meta.title: Members
meta.description: Three ways members grow every week — prepared speeches, table topics, and meeting roles — plus a full guide to Toastmasters roles and your first 90 days.

page_hero.headline: Three ways members grow every week
page_hero.intro: Every Wednesday meeting is built around three practices: prepared speeches, impromptu Table Topics, and the meeting roles that keep the room running.

headline: Three ways members grow every week

cards.title: Communication
cards.body: Develop your communication skills through a series of public speaking projects that build your fundamentals.

cards.title: Leadership
cards.body: Develop your leadership skills through meeting roles and involvement with an active Toastmasters club.

cards.title: Network
cards.body: Develop your network with like-minded entrepreneurial people. Support the businesses that matter.

role_details.heading: What each role does — and what it teaches
role_details.intro: Transcribed from the official Toastmasters International role series, "How Club Meeting Roles Build Real-World Skills."

roles.name: Chairperson
roles.summary: As the Toastmaster of the Day, you're the showrunner of the meeting, guiding the energy, pacing, and flow.
do: Receive the agenda from a club officer to start filling meeting roles.
Coordinate with the Vice President Education or General Evaluator to make sure everyone knows their role and is set up for success.
Once the meeting begins, take the lead — introducing the theme and each functionary role for the day.
Keep the energy up by guiding smooth, engaging transitions throughout the meeting.
Close the meeting by thanking participants and guests.
skills: Flexibility, adaptability, and logistics management — adapting the meeting to what is happening in the room, and adjusting to missing roles.

roles.name: Speaker
roles.summary: The Speaker shares a prepared speech with the club, bringing stories and ideas to life while sharpening their public speaking skills.
do: Deliver a prepared speech that helps others grow through your example.
Rehearse and refine your message to make it impactful.
Coordinate with your evaluator to align on goals and get meaningful feedback.
Arrive early to check mic, lighting, and setup.
skills: Manage time and pacing with precision.

roles.name: Topicsmaster
roles.summary: The Topicsmaster leads the Table Topics® session, helping members practise thinking and speaking on their feet in an impromptu setting.
do: Choose topics ahead of the meeting.
Before asking questions, explain that the role of Table Topics® is to help members improve their impromptu speaking skills and that responses should be 1–2 minutes long.
Invite members and guests from the audience to volunteer to answer a question.
skills: Plan creatively, considering the club's atmosphere, experience levels, and overall tone.
Deliver an engaging presentation that encourages participation.
Demonstrate emotional intelligence by reading the room and selecting participants appropriately.
Apply strong facilitation skills to guide the session smoothly.
Practise active listening and effectively synthesize responses.
roles.pro_tip: Volunteer to answer a Table Topics® question. It's a great way to strengthen your improvisational skills, boost critical thinking and creativity, and step outside your comfort zone.

roles.name: Speech Evaluator
roles.summary: The Speech Evaluator role is about evaluating, not judging.
do: Connect with the speaker to understand their goals.
Review the Pathways project criteria.
Prepare notes or an evaluation form.
Listen actively to the speech, taking notes on strengths and areas for improvement.
Consider key elements like structure, delivery, content, vocal variety, gestures, eye contact, and use of time.
Give a 2–3 minute evaluation.
Start with encouragement, highlighting what the speaker did well.
Offer specific, actionable suggestions for improvement.
End on a positive note, reinforcing the speaker's progress and potential.
skills: Deliver honest, constructive, and actionable feedback.
Identify and clearly articulate specific areas for improvement.
Tailor your messages to specific audiences.

roles.name: General Evaluator
roles.summary: Want to be the one who watches it all and gives the club helpful feedback at the end? Try the General Evaluator role.
do: Lead the evaluation portion of the meeting.
Oversee the evaluation team.
Confirm roles and responsibilities with each evaluator.
Observe the meeting and take notes on: timeliness, preparation, organization, enthusiasm, and execution of roles.
Deliver a verbal report evaluating the overall meeting.
skills: Ability to identify and communicate key insights

roles.name: Timer
roles.summary: The Timer keeps track of time for every speaker and meeting segment.
do: Know the time limits for each type of speaker at the meeting.
Be ready to explain timing rules and show how the time signals work.
Listen closely during the meeting and signal each speaker on time.
When asked, report each speaker's name and time.
skills: Greater awareness of timing and pacing while speaking
Supporting others with confidence and clarity
Delivering clear, concise reports based on observations

roles.name: Wordmaster (Ah-Counter & Grammarian)
roles.summary: The Wordmaster listens for filler words like "um," "ah," or "you know" that sneak into speeches and keep us from sounding our best. Also encourages club members to expand their vocabulary and speak more thoughtfully.
do: Ask the Toastmaster or a club officer for the Ah-Counter log, or be ready to take your own notes.
When introduced, briefly explain your role as the Ah-Counter.
Track filler words, overused phrases, and long pauses — for example: and, but, so, you know, ah, um.
Share your observations during the evaluation section of the meeting.
Introduce the Word of the Day and challenge members to use it during the meeting.
Listen for how language and grammar are used, including incomplete sentences, mispronunciations, grammar errors, and word mix-ups.
Take notes on each speaker's language to share helpful feedback.
Present your full report on language and grammar when called upon at the end of the meeting.
skills: Focus and attention to detail in fast-paced environments

checklists.heading: Prep checklists — 15 minutes that make the role work
checklists.intro: The difference between a role that helps you and a role that just fills a slot is about fifteen minutes of preparation. Here's the minimum for each.

groups.name: If you're speaking
items: Confirm your Pathways project and its objectives — your evaluator will be marked against them, not against your topic.
Message your evaluator with your project and one specific thing you want watched (e.g. "I over-explain; tell me where to cut").
Rehearse out loud at least twice, timed. Reading it in your head is not rehearsal.
Arrive early to check the mic, lighting, and where you'll stand.

groups.name: If you're evaluating
items: Contact the speaker before the meeting and ask what they're working on.
Read the project criteria in Pathways so your feedback is on-target.
Bring the evaluation form or your own note structure — do not improvise the structure.
Plan the shape in advance: what worked → one specific, actionable change → close on their progress.

groups.name: If you're Topicsmaster
items: Write more questions than you need, and vary them — some light, some that require a real opinion.
Tie them to the meeting theme if there is one.
Plan who you'll call first: never open with the newest member, and always leave guests an easy opt-out.

groups.name: If you're Chairperson
items: Get the agenda early and chase any unfilled roles yourself — don't assume someone else is doing it.
Prepare a short introduction for each speaker and a one-line transition between segments.
Have a plan for a no-show: know which segment you'd extend and who you'd call on.

groups.name: If you're Timer or Wordmaster
items: Know the time limits and signal system before the meeting starts — ask a club officer if you're unsure.
Prepare the one or two sentences you'll use to explain your role when introduced.
Wordmaster: choose a Word of the Day that people will plausibly use. Obscure words go unused and the exercise fails.

first_90.heading: A month-by-month plan for new members
first_90.intro: BETM addition — not official Toastmasters material.

milestones.text: Talk to the VP of Education about your communication and leadership goals.
Volunteer for Table Topics whenever you're offered. This is where confidence moves fastest.
Take a functionary role. Timer is the easiest first step and teaches you the agenda.
Deliver your Ice Breaker, the first speech in every path. It's about you, so there's nothing to research.
Give your second and third speeches, and take your first evaluation role. Ask a longer-standing member to mentor you.
